difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a necessary/sufficient confusion: the arguer treats a necessary condition for a diagnosis as though it were sufficient. Each answer choice is a dense mini-argument; two trap choices involve similar medical vocabulary but commit different errors (correlation→causation, base-rate reversal), requiring precise structural analysis.
stimulus: Elevated cortisol levels are always found in patients diagnosed with Cushing's syndrome. Dr. Petrov's patient has elevated cortisol levels. Therefore, Dr. Petrov's patient almost certainly has Cushing's syndrome.
questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A valid contract always requires the mutual assent of both parties. The agreement between Hendricks and Torwald had the mutual assent of both parties. Therefore, the agreement between Hendricks and Torwald is almost certainly a valid contract.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whenever interest rates rise sharply, consumer spending on luxury goods tends to fall. Consumer spending on luxury goods has recently fallen sharply. Therefore, interest rates have almost certainly risen sharply.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most patients who are diagnosed with lupus experience joint pain. Fernanda experiences joint pain. Therefore, Fernanda almost certainly has lupus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every architect who wins the Pritzker Prize has produced at least one widely recognized public building. Sasha has never produced a widely recognized public building. Therefore, Sasha will almost certainly never win the Pritzker Prize.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Extreme drought conditions always precede the outbreak of wildfires in this region. The region experienced extreme drought conditions last summer. Therefore, wildfires almost certainly broke out last summer.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: 'All S have P; x has P; therefore x is almost certainly S.' This confuses a necessary condition (P is necessary for S) with a sufficient condition (having P is treated as enough to conclude S). Choice A replicates this exactly: mutual assent is necessary for a valid contract, but not sufficient on its own; yet the arguer concludes the agreement is almost certainly a valid contract solely from the presence of that necessary condition.
explanations.A: Correct. 'All valid contracts require mutual assent' makes mutual assent necessary; having it doesn't guarantee validity. The argument treats the necessary condition as sufficient — identical flaw to the stimulus.
explanations.B: Close trap. This reverses a conditional ('if rates rise, spending falls' → 'spending fell, so rates rose'), which is affirming the consequent. Structurally similar but the stimulus's flaw involves a universally necessary feature being mistaken for sufficiency, not a conditional derived from a trend. Also, the stimulus's first premise is universal ('always'), while this premise is about tendency — a quantifier mismatch.
explanations.C: Different flaw — base-rate reversal. 'Most S have P; x has P; therefore x is S.' This matches the Carpaccio pattern, not the necessary-condition flaw. The stimulus's first premise is universal ('always found'), not 'most.'
explanations.D: Valid contrapositive reasoning. 'All prize-winners have P; Sasha lacks P; therefore Sasha won't win' is a legitimate modus tollens from a necessary condition. No flaw.
explanations.E: Valid reasoning. 'Drought always precedes wildfires; drought occurred; therefore wildfires occurred' correctly applies a sufficient condition (drought is sufficient for fire). This is deductively valid, not flawed.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits a part-to-whole (compositional) fallacy: properties of individual components are attributed to the whole system. Answer choices are dense five-line mini-arguments from varied domains; two traps share the structural shape superficially but reverse direction (whole-to-part) or commit a different quantifier error, demanding careful diagnosis.
stimulus: Each microprocessor in the Helion X9 server array is extraordinarily energy-efficient. Each cooling unit in the array is extraordinarily energy-efficient. Each storage module in the array is extraordinarily energy-efficient. Therefore, the Helion X9 server array as a whole is extraordinarily energy-efficient.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Glasswater Bridge was designed to be highly resilient to seismic activity. Bridges that are highly resilient to seismic activity are expensive to build. Therefore, each individual component of the Glasswater Bridge was expensive to produce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every clause in the merger agreement is legally unambiguous. Every schedule attached to the merger agreement is legally unambiguous. Every exhibit attached to the merger agreement is legally unambiguous. Therefore, the merger agreement as a whole is legally unambiguous.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The novel Westward Winds has a compelling opening chapter and a gripping climax. Since the novel's opening and climax are both compelling, the novel as a whole is almost certainly better than most novels published this decade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each musician in the Delacroix Quartet is a technically brilliant soloist. Therefore, the Delacroix Quartet performs with technically brilliant ensemble cohesion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Corvin Parliament building is considered one of the most architecturally distinguished structures in the country. Therefore, each room in the Corvin Parliament building is architecturally distinguished.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: every individual part of system X has property P; therefore the whole system X has property P. This is the compositional fallacy — inferring a property of the whole from the property of each part. Choice B replicates this precisely: every clause, every schedule, and every exhibit of the agreement is legally unambiguous; therefore the whole agreement is legally unambiguous. Legal unambiguity of all parts does not guarantee that the whole document is unambiguous (e.g., parts may interact in ambiguous ways).
explanations.A: This commits the division fallacy (whole-to-part), the reverse of composition. It also introduces a separate causal premise. Wrong direction.
explanations.B: Correct. Every individual part (clause, schedule, exhibit) has property P; therefore the whole has property P. Identical compositional fallacy to the stimulus.
explanations.C: This is a different flaw — an unwarranted comparative conclusion drawn from only two data points (opening and climax), ignoring the rest of the novel. It does not systematically enumerate all parts, which is the defining structural feature of the stimulus.
explanations.D: Closer trap — parts (individual musicians) have property P (brilliant soloists), so the whole (quartet) has P (brilliant ensemble cohesion). However, 'ensemble cohesion' is a meaningfully different property from 'technical brilliance as a soloist,' making the conclusion not just compositionally flawed but equivocating on the property itself. The stimulus attributes the very same property (energy efficiency) to the whole as to each part — no equivocation. Choice D introduces an extra layer of equivocation that the stimulus lacks.
explanations.E: Division fallacy — the whole has P, so each part has P. Reverse of the stimulus's direction.

difficultyReason: The stimulus commits an absolute-versus-percentage error: a conclusion about a higher absolute number is drawn when only a higher rate (percentage) has been established. This is among the hardest quantifier-dimension mismatches. Answer choices span economics, ecology, and history; two traps involve similar proportional language but commit base-rate or causal errors instead.
stimulus: The proportion of carbon dioxide absorbed by the Amazon rainforest that comes from industrial emissions has increased substantially over the past two decades. Therefore, the Amazon rainforest is absorbing more tons of industrial carbon dioxide today than it was twenty years ago.
questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The percentage of Doral City's municipal budget allocated to road repair has increased every year for the past five years. Therefore, Doral City is spending more dollars on road repair this year than it was five years ago.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A greater fraction of voters in Westfield County supported Candidate Rios in the most recent election than supported any other candidate. Therefore, Candidate Rios almost certainly won the election.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fraction of Pellucid Lake's fish population consisting of invasive carp has grown dramatically over the past decade. Therefore, Pellucid Lake now contains more invasive carp than it did ten years ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historically, the proportion of women enrolled in Harwick University's law school has been higher than the proportion enrolled in its medical school. Therefore, more women have graduated from Harwick's law school than from its medical school.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The share of global steel production accounted for by automated mills has risen sharply over the past decade. Therefore, the use of automated mills in steel production is likely to continue increasing in the coming decade.

explanations.correct: Stimulus flaw: a rise in the proportion (rate) of X that is Y does not entail a rise in the absolute quantity of Y, because the total amount of X could have decreased enough to offset the rate increase. Choice C replicates this exactly: a greater fraction of the lake's fish population being invasive carp does not entail more carp in absolute terms — the total fish population could have declined sharply, leaving fewer absolute carp even as the fraction grew.
explanations.A: Close trap but subtly different. A larger percentage of a budget allocated to roads does entail more absolute dollars only if the total budget stayed the same or grew — and the argument assumes this. However, unlike the stimulus, the premise concerns an annual trend ('increased every year'), and the unstated assumption about budget size is more naturally contested as a missing-premise flaw than a proportion-to-absolute error. More importantly, in the LSAT structural sense, Choice A reaches a conclusion about dollars (absolute) from a percentage — this seems like the same flaw. On closer inspection, however, the conclusion in A is about 'this year vs. five years ago,' which depends on both the rate change AND on the budget baseline, which is not ruled out as stable. The key differentiator is that Choice C's error is entirely parallel: the total population (analogous to total CO₂ absorbed) could have declined, making the absolute number lower despite a higher fraction — exactly the same logical gap as the stimulus.
explanations.B: Different flaw — a plurality (greater fraction than any other single candidate) does not establish a majority, so the election conclusion doesn't follow. This is a quantifier error (plurality vs. majority), not a proportion-to-absolute error.
explanations.C: Correct. Fraction of fish population that is invasive carp has grown → therefore more invasive carp in absolute terms. Same flaw: the total fish population could have collapsed, yielding fewer absolute carp despite a higher fraction. Identical structure to the stimulus.
explanations.D: Different flaw — comparing proportions across two groups of different sizes to draw an absolute conclusion about totals. This is a relative-vs.-absolute error, but it compares two populations rather than tracking one population's proportion over time, which is the stimulus's specific structure.
explanations.E: Different flaw — projecting a past trend into the future without justification. This is an unwarranted extrapolation, not a proportion-to-absolute error.
